raw_case_text:
A male infant was born at 26 weeks and 5 days of gestational age (GA), with a birth weight of 1,100 g (+ 0.9 SD for GA) from a CMV-seropositive mother. Pregnancy was complicated with uterine contraction for 3 days before spontaneous vaginal delivery, however, the mother's infectious episode during pregnancy was not reported. His Apgar scores were 1 at 1 min and 1 at 5 min. He was initially treated for respiratory distress syndrome, dyspepsia and symptomatic patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). Indomethacin and inotropic support using dopamine and dobutamine were started from day of life (DOL)1. However, indomethacin was not effective and the infant was transferred to our hospital at DOL3 for surgical treatment of PDA. Physical examination on admission was not remarkable for microcephaly (head circumference: 25.0 cm [+ 0.7 SD for GA]), hepatosplenomegaly, rash, jaundice and any neurologic signs. The initial laboratory testing did not show abnormal findings including anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated liver enzymes or conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (Table 1). Blood coagulation was not remarkable for the infant's prematurity (i.e., prothrombin time: 1,31 INR; fibrinogen: 112 mg/dl; d-dimer: 2.74 mug/ml). Head ultrasound did not reveal any abnormalities such as periventricular calcifications. On the day of admission, he underwent the ligation of PDA and was stabilized hemodynamically. Formula milk feeding was started on DOL4 and then unpasteurized breast milk was added from DOL7. However, dyspepsia persisted and abdominal distention appeared and enteral feeding was stopped at DOL7. Despite being fasted and treated with hyperosmolar enemas from DOL7, the effect was limited. At DOL8, bilious residuals were collected from the nasogastric tube and abdominal radiography showed pneumoperitoneum (Figure 1A). Emergent laparotomy revealed a perforation of the terminal ileum on the mesenteric side, which is opposite to predilection site of NEC, and resection of the perforated site with ileostomy construction was performed. The infant received transfusion of packed red blood cells during the operation at DOL8. Pathological examination of the resected ileum revealed non-specific inflammatory changes which were consistent with enterocolitis and CMV inclusion bodies were not identified (Figure 3a). After the operation, dyspepsia persisted and hepatic transaminases were elevated from DOL14 (Figure 2). Abdominal distension appeared again at DOL17 and abdominal radiography showed recurrence of pneumoperitoneum (Figure 1B). He underwent laparotomy and a perforation was found just proximal to the ileostomy. Serum anti-CMV IgG and IgM, that was performed for the differential diagnosis for the elevated hepatic transaminases, were both positive at DOL28. Pathological examination of the second operation, which was reported at DOL30, showed characteristic CMV intranuclear inclusion bodies in the endothelium of lamia propria (Figure 3b). Immunostaining for CMV with the intestinal specimen at the first surgery on DOL8, which was performed retrospectively after the result of pathological examination of the second operation was reported, demonstrated small amount of CMV positive cells (Figure 3d). CMV-DNA was also detected in both blood and urine at DOL28. Moreover, CMV-DNA was detected in the dried umbilical cord, which was obtained within a week from birth and traditionally preserved at the obstetric clinic in Japan as a precious keepsake to parents, suggesting prenatal transmission of CMV from his mother.
Although there are no clinical trials suggesting the benefit of GCV for CMV infections in the preterm neonates (e.g., gestational age <= 32 weeks or weighing <=1,200 g at the onset of treatment) or CMV-associated intestinal disease in the neonates, we chose the treatment with intravenous GCV 12 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks, considering the severity and persistence of the disease and the result of the viral study suggesting the congenital infection of CMV. After starting GCV therapy at DOL34, dyspepsia and abdominal distension resolved and CMV-DNA in the blood was concurrently decreased to lower than detection level by DOL70 (Blood CMV-DNA: 1.3 x 107 [copies/mL] at DOL 28; 3.6 x 106 at DOL 35; 6.2 x 104 at DOL 56; 2.9 x 104 at DOL 63; less than detection level at DOL 70 and 77, Figure 2). No recurrence of gastrointestinal symptoms had occurred thereafter and the ileostomy was closed at 3 months of life. CMV inclusion body or CMV immunoreactivity were not detected in the resection specimen at the final ileostomy closure (Figures 3c,e). During GCV therapy, transient and spontaneously recovered neutropenia was observed around 4 weeks after the initiation of GCV therapy (Table 1). No other acute toxicity of ganciclovir including anemia, thrombocytopenia, liver dysfunction or renal dysfunction was not encountered during and after GCV treatment (Table 1). No abnormal finding with electroencephalography, brain magnetic resonance imaging and auditory brainstem response audiometry were noted before discharge. He was discharged from the hospital at 5 months of life and had been doing well without any neurodevelopmental sequelae noted during the 5-year follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: An extremely preterm male neonate born at 26 weeks 5 days' gestation (birth weight 1,100 g) to a CMV-seropositive mother developed persistent feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, and recurrent ileal perforations on days of life 8 and 17.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born via spontaneous vaginal delivery at 26w5d gestation (Apgar 1 and 1 at 1 and 5 min) after 3 days of preterm uterine contractions, the infant was transferred on day of life (DOL) 3 for surgical ligation of an indomethacin-refractory patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). Formula feeds were started on DOL 4 and unpasteurized maternal breast milk was added on DOL 7, when abdominal distension and dyspepsia required stopping feeds. On DOL 8, bilious nasogastric residuals and pneumoperitoneum prompted emergency laparotomy, resection of a mesenteric-side terminal ileal perforation, ileostomy creation, and PRBC transfusion. Elevated transaminases developed on DOL 14, and recurrent abdominal distension and pneumoperitoneum on DOL 17 required a second laparotomy for a perforation just proximal to the ileostomy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Extreme prematurity (26 weeks 5 days' gestation, birth weight 1,100 g [+0.9 SD]), respiratory distress syndrome, and symptomatic patent ductus arteriosus status post surgical ligation on DOL 3; born to a CMV-seropositive mother.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent dyspepsia/feeding intolerance, bilious residuals, abdominal distension, and recurrent bowel perforations (DOL 8 and DOL 17).

objective.physical_examination: On DOL 3 admission: head circumference 25.0 cm (+0.7 SD, normocephalic), no hepatosplenomegaly, rash, jaundice, or neurological signs. On DOL 7-8 and DOL 17: marked abdominal distension and bilious nasogastric aspirates.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial DOL 3 labs: no anemia, thrombocytopenia, transaminitis, or conjugated hyperbilirubinemia; coagulation appropriate for prematurity (INR 1.31, fibrinogen 112 mg/dL, D-dimer 2.74 ug/mL). Progressive elevation of hepatic transaminases from DOL 14. On DOL 28, serum anti-CMV IgG and IgM were both positive. Cranial ultrasound was normal without periventricular calcifications; abdominal radiographs on DOL 8 and DOL 17 demonstrated frank pneumoperitoneum.
objective.advanced_workup: First laparotomy (DOL 8) resected ileum showed non-specific enterocolitis on routine H&E, but retrospective anti-CMV immunostaining identified sparse CMV-positive cells. Second laparotomy (DOL 17, reported DOL 30) resected ileum proximal to the ileostomy demonstrated characteristic cytomegalovirus (CMV) intranuclear inclusion bodies in lamina propria endothelial cells. At DOL 28, CMV-DNA PCR was positive in both blood (1.3 x 10^7 copies/mL) and urine, and retrospective PCR of the preserved dried umbilical cord (collected within 1 week of birth) was positive for CMV-DNA, confirming congenital in utero CMV transmission. Pre-discharge brain MRI, EEG, and auditory brainstem response (ABR) audiometry were all normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) enterocolitis presenting with recurrent terminal ileal perforations (DOL 8 and DOL 17) and hepatitis in an extremely preterm infant, confirmed by lamina propria endothelial CMV intranuclear inclusions and positive CMV immunostaining in resected ileal specimens, positive serum CMV IgM/IgG, high blood CMV-DNA load (1.3 x 10^7 copies/mL on DOL 28), and positive dried umbilical cord CMV-DNA PCR. Treated with a 6-week course of intravenous ganciclovir (12 mg/kg/day starting on DOL 34; complicated only by transient self-recovering neutropenia at week 4), resulting in resolution of abdominal distension, progressive clearance of blood CMV-DNA to undetectable levels by DOL 70, successful ileostomy closure at 3 months of life (with negative CMV histology/IHC in the closure specimen), and intact neurodevelopment without sequelae at 5-year follow-up.
